label: Real run on this Mac's Docker Compose stack, with synthetic traffic from klaxon.traffic: synthetic data, a simulated provider, no real money. One fault from klaxon.faults, pool-exhaustion, was injected on purpose. The alert was raised by klaxon.alerts from what the stack showed. Klaxon's loop ran live on it, through Claude Code on Aravind's seat, and stopped on diagnosed after 9 steps; any reply it got is a recorded response, not a simulation. It was offered one write action (rollback_deploy), as in week 4; in an evaluation run its gate only plans an action the diagnosis names: nobody is asked, and nothing runs. The diagnosis was compared with the fault's recorded cause by a rule (klaxon.grading), not by a person or a model. Its diagnosis named no action, so nobody was asked to approve one. The fault's cause was removed by the harness's clearing (klaxon.faults).

case.name: pool-exhaustion
case.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
case.right_answer: The fault's recorded cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500.
case.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

fault.name: pool-exhaustion
fault.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
fault.cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500
expected_symptoms: the pool runs dry about 40 to 50 s after the deploy; then POST /payments takes 5 to 8 s (a worker thread, then the pool's 5 s wait) and fails with a 500: the p95 latency passes 7 s, and the 5xx share passes 70% within a minute
the payments API logs 'unhandled error' with PoolTimeout: no connection within 5 s
its health check fails too, so docker marks it unhealthy, while PostgreSQL itself is up
the traffic's clients retry and give up: many payments end with their outcome unknown, and arrivals past 64 in flight are shed
the money check passes: a payment that never got a connection was never charged, and one charged before its answer was lost is confirmed by its webhook
fault.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

diagnosis.hypothesis: The payments-api container was recreated at 07:29:54 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept (the only payments-api setting I can tie to the timing), and right after that the service started failing with psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout. Requests wait about 5 s for a Postgres connection and then return 500. This fits a DB connection pool that is exhausted, probably because connections are held and not released. Both POST /payments and POST /payments/{id}/refunds fail, and that explains the 5xx rate and the high p95 latency. I did not confirm what holds the connections, and I did not confirm that REFUND_CONNECTION=kept is the cause. It is the leading suspect only because it is the setting that changed and the timing matches.

evidence.shows: The symptom is real: 500s on payments-api rose from 0.15/s to 3.44/s at about 07:31 while 201s fell.
Every payments-api error log is a PoolTimeout (psycopg_pool) on POST /payments, i.e. no DB connection became free in time.

payments-api was redeployed at 07:29:54 with PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents and REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, about a minute before the 500s began. Other services were created earlier at 07:28:28.

A failing POST /payments trace takes 5.09 s with a gap of about 5 s between the first Redis SET and the later Redis EVAL, then ends with PoolTimeout. The request waited for a DB connection and none was free.
Provider calls stay fast (p95 about 5 ms), so a slow provider does not explain the pool exhaustion.
Refund route 500s rose at the same time as the payment 500s, so the fault is shared across routes in payments-api, not specific to charges.
A refund trace shows a PoolTimeout too: 7.4 s, with about 2.4 s passing before the first Redis SET and about 5 s more before the EVAL. Requests are waiting on the DB pool on both routes.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll payments-api back to the settings it had before the 07:29:54 deploy. Then check that PoolTimeout errors stop and 5xx drops below the threshold. If they continue, look at the Postgres connection count and what holds the connections (long transactions, or connections kept open across refund calls).

diagnosis.blast_radius: payments-api restarts and pauses briefly, so in-flight payment and refund requests fail during the restart. The rollback undoes the other settings from that deploy too (PROVIDER_BREAKER, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT), and I did not inspect those. It repairs nothing already booked. I did not run the money check, so I cannot say whether any payments or refunds are wrong.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: If the rollback makes things worse, redeploy payments-api with the settings from 07:29:54 (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=kept) and look at Postgres directly.
